blocks.text: 1. overview
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059636-425239521.png

MAE, MSE, RMSE, and RMSLE, the four metrics covered so far in this module, all measure error directly, in some raw unit, squared unit, or log-transformed unit. R Squared, also written R², takes a genuinely different approach to the same underlying evaluation problem, answering not how big is the typical error, but how much of the target variable's natural variation does the model actually manage to explain, expressed as a single, dimensionless number that stays comparable across entirely different problems and scales.

This shift in framing, from raw error size to explained variance, makes R² one of the most widely reported, and sometimes most widely misunderstood, metrics in all of regression evaluation, and understanding precisely what it measures, and just as importantly, what it does not measure, is the focus of this topic.
2. Formalizing the Naive Baseline Comparison
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059636-359709535.png

The MAE topic, covered earlier in this module, introduced a practical technique worth recalling directly: comparing a model's MAE against a naive baseline, one that simply predicts the target's overall mean for every single example, to give the raw MAE value real, judgable context and meaning.

R² takes this exact same idea and builds it directly into the metric's own formula, rather than requiring it to be computed separately as an extra, optional step. Every R² calculation automatically, inherently compares the actual model's performance against precisely this same naive mean-prediction baseline, meaning the comparison this course already recommended doing manually for MAE is simply built in, by design, whenever R² is used at all.
3. The Formula

R² is built from two quantities. The first, called the sum of squared residuals, is the total squared error the actual trained model makes across every example, essentially an unaveraged version of the numerator inside MSE, already covered in depth two topics ago. The second, called the total sum of squares, is the total squared error a naive baseline model, one that always predicts the target's overall mean, would make across those exact same examples.

R² is then computed as 1 minus the ratio of the sum of squared residuals divided by the total sum of squares. This single formula directly expresses how much better the actual model performs compared to the naive mean-prediction baseline: if the model's errors are much smaller than the baseline's errors, that ratio is small, and R² lands close to 1; if the model's errors are comparable to or larger than the baseline's errors, that ratio approaches or exceeds 1, and R² lands close to 0 or even goes negative.
4. Reading an R² Value
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059636-130572685.png

R² values have a clean, well-defined interpretation across their range. A value of exactly 1.0 means the model explains 100 percent of the target's variance, corresponding to perfect predictions with zero error anywhere. A value of exactly 0.0 means the model explains precisely 0 percent of the variance, performing no better, in aggregate, than simply predicting the naive mean baseline for every single example, regardless of the actual input features.

A negative R² value, covered in more depth in its own section shortly, means the model actually performs worse than that naive mean-prediction baseline, a genuinely concerning result. A more typical real-world R² value, something like 0.75, means the model explains 75 percent of the target's natural variance, leaving the remaining 25 percent unexplained, whether due to genuine randomness in the data, missing predictive features, or limitations in the model itself.

blocks.text: 5. What Variance Explained Actually Means

R²'s framing connects directly back to variance, a concept already covered in depth in the Statistical Summary and Distribution Analysis topics earlier in this course. The target variable's total variance describes how naturally spread out its true values are across the dataset, entirely independent of any model at all, simply a property of the data itself.

R² asks a precise question about that natural spread: what fraction of it does the model's predictions actually account for, or explain, through its use of the input features? This is a genuinely different lens than MAE or RMSE's direct focus on raw error size, since it frames model quality relative to how much natural variation existed in the target to begin with, rather than in absolute, standalone terms.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A target with very little natural variance to begin with, one where almost every true value is already close to the mean, makes achieving a high R² considerably easier, since there is less variation for any model, even a weak one, to fail to explain in the first place.

blocks.text: 6. A Genuine Strength: Scale Independence
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059637-218903812.png

The MAE topic closed by identifying a real limitation: MAE values depend entirely on the target's scale and units, making them impossible to compare directly across different problems without additional context. R² has exactly the opposite property, and this is one of its most valuable practical strengths: it is dimensionless, with no units attached at all, and it always falls somewhere between negative infinity and a maximum of 1, regardless of what the underlying target actually measures or what scale it is expressed in.

An R² of 0.8 carries the exact same meaning, explains 80 percent of the target's variance, whether the underlying model is predicting house prices in dollars, rainfall in millimeters, or exam scores on a 100-point scale. This scale independence makes R² directly comparable across entirely different problems and target types in a way that MAE, RMSE, and even RMSLE, all covered earlier in this module, simply cannot achieve on their own.
7. Understanding Negative R²
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059637-374170575.png

A model producing a negative R² is performing worse, on the evaluation data, than the trivially simple strategy of always predicting the target's overall mean, regardless of the actual input features for any given example. This can genuinely happen in practice, most commonly through severe overfitting to training data that fails to generalize at all to new data, or through evaluating a model on data that looks meaningfully different from anything it was ever trained on.

A negative R² should be treated as a strong, unmistakable warning sign, not merely a below-average or disappointing score. It indicates the model is actively worse than doing nothing at all, worse than the simplest possible naive baseline, and it warrants immediate, careful investigation into what specifically went wrong, whether a genuine bug in the modeling pipeline, a serious train-test distribution mismatch, or a fundamentally unsuitable choice of algorithm for the problem at hand.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Negative R² most commonly shows up when evaluating a model on a test set that differs substantially from its training data, or when a model has badly overfit. Seeing it should trigger an immediate check of the entire data pipeline and train-test split, not just a shrug and a note that the model performed poorly.

blocks.text: 8. A Known Weakness: Rewarding Added Features

blocks.alt: A Known Weakness: Rewarding Added Features
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059637-887339654.png

R², as defined and computed in this topic, has a specific, systematic weakness worth understanding clearly before moving to the next topic: adding any additional feature to a model, evaluated on the exact same training data used to fit it, can never actually decrease R², and in practice it very often increases at least slightly, even when that added feature is genuinely useless, containing no real predictive information about the target whatsoever.

This happens because an additional feature gives the model strictly more flexibility to fit the training data's specific patterns, including its noise, even if that flexibility does not correspond to any genuine, generalizable improvement in predictive power. This creates a real, systematic bias: plain R², computed this way, rewards adding more features to a model regardless of whether those features actually help, which is precisely the exact problem Adjusted R², the very next topic in this module, was specifically designed to correct.
9. When R² Is the Right Metric to Report

blocks.alt: When R² Is the Right Metric to Report
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059882-898522777.png

R² is the natural choice whenever a single, scale-independent summary of overall model quality is needed, particularly when comparing genuinely different models across genuinely different problems or target scales, exactly the comparability advantage covered earlier in this topic. It is also the standard, expected metric in scientific and academic reporting, where communicating precisely how much of an observed phenomenon a model actually captures is often the central question being asked.

R² is additionally a fast, effective screening tool for catching a genuinely broken or actively harmful model quickly: a negative R² is an immediate, unmistakable red flag that demands investigation, in a way that a merely elevated MAE or RMSE value might not communicate quite as unambiguously to someone quickly scanning results.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example

The example below computes R² for a trained model, compares it directly against the naive mean-prediction baseline it is built around, and demonstrates the feature-addition bias covered in this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(100, 1))
y = 3 * X.ravel() + rng.normal(0, 2, size=100)

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)
predictions = model.predict(X)

r2 = r2_score(y, predictions)
print("Model R2:", round(r2, 3))

# Confirm this matches predicting the mean as the baseline (R2 = 0 by definition)
naive_predictions = np.full_like(y, y.mean())
naive_r2 = r2_score(y, naive_predictions)
print("Naive baseline R2:", round(naive_r2, 3), "(always exactly 0, by definition)")

# Demonstrate the feature-addition bias: add a genuinely useless random feature
X_with_noise_feature = np.column_stack([X, rng.normal(0, 1, size=100)])
model_with_noise = LinearRegression()
model_with_noise.fit(X_with_noise_feature, y)
r2_with_noise = r2_score(y, model_with_noise.predict(X_with_noise_feature))
print(f"\nR2 with a genuinely useless extra feature added: {r2_with_noise:.4f}")
print(f"Original R2 without that feature: {r2:.4f}")
print("Notice R2 did not decrease, despite the added feature carrying no real information")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The naive baseline's R² is always exactly 0 by mathematical definition, since it is precisely the reference point the entire R² formula is built around, exactly the built-in baseline comparison covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: R² measures how much of the target's variance a model explains, rather than measuring raw error size directly.
It builds the naive mean-prediction baseline comparison directly into its formula, rather than requiring it as a separate step.
R² ranges from negative infinity up to 1, with 1 meaning perfect predictions and 0 meaning no better than the naive baseline.
A negative R² means the model performs worse than simply guessing the mean, a serious warning sign demanding investigation.
It is dimensionless and scale-independent, making it directly comparable across entirely different problems and target scales.
This is the direct opposite of MAE's scale-dependence limitation covered earlier in this module.
Adding any feature to a model can never decrease R² on training data, even a genuinely useless one, a systematic bias.
It fits cross-problem comparisons, scientific reporting, and quick screening for a genuinely broken or harmful model.
Next up: Adjusted R², which corrects this exact feature-addition bias by explicitly penalizing model complexity.
